title: Children's medicines: weight-based dosing, formulations and ten-fold errors
blurb: Check a child's dose from an accurate weight in kilograms, measure liquids safely with oral syringes and catch the ten-fold errors that harm children.
question: Jamie, 3, weighs 14 kg and is prescribed IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg once daily. The prescription reads 980 mg. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Children range from a 500 g preterm baby to a 90 kg teenager, so one dose cannot fit all. Formally, most children's doses are calculated from body weight (mg/kg) or body surface area and checked against the BNF for Children (BNFC). Plain English: an accurate weight in kilograms is the foundation of every paediatric dose, and every calculation is checked, because a slipped decimal point can give ten times the intended amount.

teach.caption: Do not use an estimated, remembered or converted weight (stones and pounds) for dosing.

head: Step
Formula
Example
teach.caption: Always check the daily total and the maximum, not just the single dose.

teach.body: Before giving any dose, ask: does this look right for this child? Compare the dose with the usual range, the volume with what you would expect, and the child's dose with the adult dose. A weight-based dose should not normally exceed the usual adult dose, which matters in large adolescents. If anything looks wrong by a factor of ten, stop and query it with the prescriber before giving it.
teach.cite: BNFC prescribing in children; NMC Code 18

teach.caption: NPSA alert 2007/19: measure and give oral liquids with oral syringes. Giving an oral or enteral medicine by an IV route is a Never Event.

teach.h: Giving a medicine to a child
items: Positively identify the child (name band, date of birth) and check allergies.
Check the prescription: name, form, route, strength, dose, time, weight recorded.
Check the calculation and have it independently checked where policy requires.
Choose an age-appropriate formulation and explain to the child and parent.
Record the dose given, withheld or refused, with the reason.

teach.text: A father saying his son weighed 'about two and a half stone' a few months ago is not a dosing weight. Children grow quickly and conversions invite errors. Weigh the child now and record the weight in kilograms.

teach.h: Scenario: Jamie, 3, on the children's ward
teach.body: Jamie weighs 14 kg and is prescribed IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg once daily. The chart reads 980 mg. Nurse Tom calculates 7 × 14 = 98 mg: the prescription is ten times too high, a classic decimal error. He does not prepare the dose, contacts the prescriber to correct it, checks the corrected 98 mg with a second nurse, and reports the near miss so the team can learn from it.
teach.cite: Weight-based dosing; NICE NG5 1.1.7 (report medicines incidents)

items: Weigh on admission and record in kg; do not dose from estimated or old weights.
Dose = mg/kg × kg; volume = (wanted ÷ stock) × volume.
Check single dose, daily total and maximum; not normally above the adult dose.
Ten-fold errors: decimal point, mg vs micrograms, wrong concentration.
Oral liquids by oral or enteral syringe; oral medicines given IV is a Never Event.

summary: You can now calculate and sense-check a weight-based dose and a liquid volume for a child, and spot ten-fold errors before they reach the child. You can also choose the right syringe and formulation and follow safe administration checks.

A.q: Jamie, 3, weighs 14 kg and is prescribed IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg once daily. The prescription reads 980 mg. What should the nurse do?
options: Give 98 mg and record the change
Give half the dose and recheck
A.why: 7 mg/kg × 14 kg = 98 mg. 980 mg is ten times too high. The nurse must not give it and must ask the prescriber to correct the prescription.

whyNot.0: The prescription is a ten-fold overdose.
whyNot.1: A nurse cannot alter a prescription; the prescriber must correct it.
whyNot.3: Half of 980 mg is still five times the correct dose, and doses are not altered without a prescription.

A.q: Leo, 4, is admitted for IV antibiotics. His father says Leo weighed 'about two and a half stone' a few months ago. What should the nurse do before medicines are prescribed?
options: Convert 2.5 stone to kg and record it
Use the weight in his GP record
Weigh Leo now and record it in kg
A.why: Children's doses depend on an accurate current weight, so weigh the child on admission and record it in kilograms.

whyNot.0: Converting an old, estimated weight from stones invites error.
whyNot.1: Age-based estimates are less accurate than a measured weight when the child can be weighed.
whyNot.2: A previous recorded weight may be out of date in a growing child.

A.q: Maya, 18 months, is prescribed oral paracetamol suspension. The only syringes in the clean utility are IV (Luer) syringes. What should the nurse use?
options: A medicine spoon from the kitchen
An oral or enteral syringe from pharmacy
A medicine pot with the dose estimated
A.why: Oral liquids should be measured and given with oral or enteral syringes, which cannot connect to IV devices (NPSA 2007/19).

whyNot.0: Using IV syringes for oral liquids creates a wrong-route risk, even if labelled.
whyNot.1: Spoons are inaccurate for small paediatric volumes.
whyNot.3: An estimated volume in a pot is inaccurate for a small child.

B.q: Sami, 2, is prescribed paracetamol oral suspension 180 mg. The stock is 120 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be given?

whyNot.1: 3.3 mL comes from inverting the formula (120 ÷ 180 × 5).
whyNot.2: 6 mL does not follow from the stock strength.
whyNot.3: 1.5 is the ratio before multiplying by the 5 mL stock volume.

B.q: Grace, 6, weighs 20 kg. A medicine is prescribed at 15 mg/kg every 4 hours, six doses a day. The BNFC maximum is 75 mg/kg per day. What should the nurse conclude?
options: Safe: the daily total is 1,500 mg
Unsafe: the daily total is 1,800 mg
Unsafe: 300 mg exceeds the single dose
B.why: Each dose is 15 × 20 = 300 mg; six doses = 1,800 mg a day. The maximum is 75 × 20 = 1,500 mg a day, so the regimen exceeds it.

whyNot.0: The single dose is correct, but the daily total must also be checked.
whyNot.1: 1,500 mg is the maximum, not the prescribed total of 1,800 mg.
whyNot.3: 300 mg matches 15 mg/kg; the problem is the daily total.

B.q: Finn, 8 months, is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms orally. The stock elixir is 50 micrograms per mL. What volume should be given?

whyNot.0: 12.5 mL is ten times the correct volume: a decimal error.
whyNot.3: 0.125 mL is one tenth of the correct volume.

C.q: Kai, 16, weighs 92 kg. A medicine is prescribed at 10 mg/kg per dose, giving 920 mg. The usual adult dose is 500 mg. What should the nurse do?
options: Give 920 mg as it matches his weight
Query it, as it is above the adult dose
Give 500 mg and inform the prescriber later
C.why: A weight-calculated dose should not normally exceed the adult dose. 920 mg is almost double, so the prescriber must review it before anything is given.

whyNot.0: Weight-based dosing in a large adolescent can exceed the adult dose, which is not normally given.
whyNot.2: Nurses cannot substitute a different dose without a prescription.
whyNot.3: Monitoring does not make an excessive dose safe.

C.q: Ava, 2, weighs 12 kg. Her oral morphine is prescribed as 24 mg. The ward guideline dose is 200 micrograms/kg. What should the nurse recognise?
options: The dose is correct for her weight
It is ten times the expected dose
It is one tenth of the expected dose
It is correct if split over the day
C.why: 200 micrograms/kg × 12 kg = 2,400 micrograms = 2.4 mg. 24 mg is ten times that: a classic decimal or units slip. Withhold and query the prescriber.

whyNot.0: The expected dose is 2.4 mg, not 24 mg.
whyNot.2: One tenth of the expected dose would be 0.24 mg.
whyNot.3: Splitting does not correct a ten-fold overdose; the guideline gives a per-dose figure.

C.q: Before giving Ella, 5, her oral medicine, a nurse realises she has drawn it up in an IV syringe. She has not given it. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Redraw it and report the near miss
Redraw it; near misses need no report
Give it, as the dose is correct
Raise it at her next annual appraisal
C.why: The dose should be redrawn in an oral syringe, and the near miss reported through the incident system so the team can learn (NICE NG5 1.1.7: report all medicines incidents). An oral medicine in an IV syringe is a wrong-route risk.

whyNot.1: Near misses are medicines incidents and should be reported.
whyNot.2: Giving it from an IV syringe keeps the wrong-route risk; oral syringes are required.
whyNot.3: Delaying to an appraisal loses the chance for timely learning.

reteach.title: Weigh, work out, wonder
reteach.question: What three habits stop most paediatric dosing errors?

blocks.body: Weigh: a measured weight in kg, today. Work out: dose = mg/kg × kg, then volume, then daily total, checked against BNFC. Wonder: does this look right? If the volume is ten times what you expect, or the dose is above the adult dose, stop and query before giving.

blocks.text: The nurse never 'corrects' a wrong prescription by giving a different dose. Withhold the dose and ask the prescriber to change the prescription.

explain.body: Multiply the dose per kg by the weight in kg. Then check the frequency and multiply to get the daily total, and compare it with the BNFC maximum.

test.q: Ruby weighs 18 kg and is prescribed 10 mg/kg. What is her single dose?

whyNot.0: 1,800 mg is ten times too high.
whyNot.1: 18 mg is one tenth of the dose.

explain.body: Volume = (dose wanted ÷ stock strength) × stock volume. Sense check: if the dose is more than the stock strength, the volume is more than the stock volume.

test.q: A child needs 60 mg. The stock is 120 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be drawn up?

whyNot.0: 10 mL is from inverting the formula.
whyNot.2: 0.5 is the ratio before multiplying by 5 mL.
whyNot.3: 5 mL would give 120 mg, double the dose.

explain.body: Misplaced decimal points, mg and micrograms confused, or the wrong concentration picked from two strengths can each multiply or divide the dose by ten or more. A weight entered in pounds instead of kilograms gives a dose 2.2 times too high.

test.q: A prescription reads 'digoxin 500 mg' for a baby. The usual dose is in micrograms. What type of error is most likely?
test.why: Writing mg instead of micrograms gives a dose 1,000 times too high: a units error.

whyNot.0: The route is not in question.
whyNot.1: The frequency is not the issue described.

explain.body: Oral and enteral liquids go in oral or enteral (ENFit) syringes, which cannot connect to IV devices. An oral or enteral medicine given by a parenteral route is a Never Event.

test.q: Why are oral or enteral syringes used for liquid medicines in children?
options: They are cheaper than IV syringes
They are sterile, unlike IV syringes
They cannot connect to IV lines
test.why: Oral and enteral syringes are designed so they cannot connect to IV devices, preventing wrong-route errors.

whyNot.0: Volume is not the safety reason.
whyNot.2: Sterility is not the safety feature; the connector is.
